answer_text:
Let

\[
I(y)=\int_0^y \frac{dx}{(x-1)\ln x}, \qquad y\to 1^-.
\]

We estimate both factors using only elementary inequalities.

For \(0<x<1\), the standard logarithmic inequality

\[
\ln x \le x-1
\]

holds. Since \(x-1<0\), multiplying reverses the inequality:

\[
(x-1)\ln x \ge (x-1)^2=(1-x)^2.
\]

Thus, for \(0<x<y<1\),

\[
0<\frac{1}{(x-1)\ln x}\le \frac{1}{(1-x)^2}.
\]

Therefore

\[
0\le I(y)\le \int_0^y \frac{dx}{(1-x)^2}
= \left[\frac{1}{1-x}\right]_0^y
= \frac{1}{1-y}-1.
\]

Now estimate the prefactor. For \(y<1\), \(\ln y<y-1\), so \(1-y+\ln y<0\). Hence

\[
|1-y+\ln y|=-(1-y+\ln y)=y-1-\ln y.
\]

Using the integral form of the logarithm,

\[
y-1-\ln y=\int_y^1 \left(\frac1t-1\right)\,dt.
\]

For \(t\in[y,1]\) with \(y>1/2\), we have \(1/t\le 2\), so

\[
\frac1t-1=\frac{1-t}{t}\le 2(1-t).
\]

Thus

\[
|1-y+\ln y|
\le 2\int_y^1 (1-t)\,dt
=(1-y)^2.
\]

Combining the two estimates, with \(a=1-y\),

\[
\left|(1-y+\ln y)I(y)\right|
\le a^2\left(\frac1a-1\right)
=a(1-a)\to 0
\qquad\text{as }y\to 1^-.
\]

By the squeeze theorem,

\[
\boxed{0}
\]
